Lean statements · FlashProve

What an accepted proof shows: the statement, the model, the verifier

Statements and definitions of FlashProve's Lean library, explained in words next to their Lean code.
Each card shows one declaration in rows: words on the left, its Lean code on the right, without the docstring above it (that is in the side panel); a theorem's code ends at the sign that opens its proof. Hover a Lean name to read its declaration in place; click to open it in the side panel.

What the Lean verification establishes. The Lean library puts together the following items.

  • (1) Model. A formally defined integer quantization modelNextToken of the model being served, as a function from weights and a list of tokens to the next token (§2, Appendix C).
  • (2) IOP. An interactive oracle proof flashProve for the claim that given output tokens are this model's output on a given prompt, at committed weights. It is formalized as a holographic IOP (§3, Appendix A).
  • (3) Compilation. The BCS compilation compile (flashProve setup) of (2) in the random oracle model (§4).
  • (4) Security. Proofs that (3) is complete, sound and statistically zero knowledge in the random oracle model. Formally, these are the six theorems in Final statements, which hold for public files that form a public setup (A public setup).
  • (5) Hash function. A definition of BLAKE2b in Lean, and blake2bHash, the hash function on bit strings built from it (Appendix B).
  • (6) Fiat–Shamir verifier. leanVerifier, which the cards call the Lean verifier: the verifier of (3) with blake2bHash in place of the random oracle (its definition is in Final statements). Under the Fiat–Shamir heuristic it inherits the soundness proved in (4).
  • (7) Executable verifier. executableVerifier, a Lean function that can be run and is proved to return the verdict of leanVerifier (the theorem executableVerifier_eq_leanVerifier, also in Final statements).

Goals. FlashProve's code is cryptographic and was largely written by AI systems. Formal verification is meant to make its security independent of trust in that code. Items (1) to (4) specify the protocol in Lean and prove completeness, soundness and zero knowledge in the random oracle model (the precise forms are under “The statements, at a glance”, below). The following gaps remain.

  • The statements must say what is meant. Lean does not check this. A person has to read the statements and the definitions under them, and this page is for that.
  • The programs that run must implement (3). How this is addressed depends on the property.
    • Soundness depends on the verifier alone. Items (5) to (7) provide one that can be run. Nothing is proved about the faster C++ verifier.
    • Completeness concerns honest parties and can be tested: run a prover, then the verifier of (7) on its output (Running the verifier).
    • Zero knowledge depends on the prover alone. A prover program has to be audited against the honest prover of (3), which is a Lean definition that cannot be run and of which this page shows only part (§6).

In particular, a reader who only needs to trust the verifier has to:

  • read the definition Sound (§1) and the theorem sound of (4);
  • read the definitions of the compiler's verifier in (3) (§4.2, §4.3) and the definition (6);
  • read the theorem executableVerifier_eq_leanVerifier of (7);
  • skim the definitions of the model (1) and of BLAKE2b (5);
  • check the conditions on the public files (A public setup); the verifier does not test that they specify exact match.

That executableVerifier is then sound is a conclusion, not a theorem. By the theorem of (7) it returns the verdict of leanVerifier on the files of a public setup, and that leanVerifier is sound rests on the Fiat–Shamir heuristic of (6) and on assumptions listed in §11. The conclusion is about the Lean function executableVerifier; what a run of the command lean-verify adds to it is described in Running the verifier.

Checking the proofs yourself. To check the proofs, go to the directory lean/ of this repository and run lake exe cache get && LEAN_ABORT_ON_PANIC=1 lake build to compile and type-check the library. A build does not fail on an unfinished proof or on an added axiom. For these, and for a second check of every compiled module by Lean's kernel, run python3 -B scripts/check.py afterwards: it rebuilds the library in a scratch copy, replays it in the kernel and verifies that no declaration depends on an axiom other than Lean's standard ones (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound). On the machine used for this release (84 cores, 960 GiB of memory) the script took four and a half hours; lean/CHECKING.md gives the steps, the requirements and what a pass shows. For standard guidelines see the chapter “Validating a Lean Proof” of the Lean reference manual (lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/ValidatingProofs/). Lean's kernel is trusted, not proved correct, and the pinned version, 4.29.1, predates fixes for publicly known soundness bugs in the kernel (§11).

Further down

  • A public setup, in “What the theorems refer to”, lists the conditions. The library defines one public setup, namely the public files of a stored example with synthetic weights.
  • Running the verifier says what the command lean-verify evaluates, what is proved about it, where files are parsed, what is trusted, and what was run.
  • §4 opens with the definitions of the compiler's verifier.
  • Limits and gaps are listed in §11, lean/LIMITS.md and lean/GAPS.md. §11 also says what this page contains and what it does not show.

Final statements

Six theorems (the repository's other pages call them the six lines) and one definition, the Lean verifier, about one argument system, compile (flashProve setup). In each of them:

  • setup is a public setup (PublicSetup): three public files that meet four conditions (see A public setup below and FilesInUse in §4.4);
  • flashProve setup is the input of compile for these files.

Both are described on cards in the next section.

The six theorems:

TheoremSoundnessAtFullSide/Face/TheSixLines.lean:93

In Lean · AtFullSide/Face/TheSixLines.lean, lines 93–93
Given, then
  • a public setup setup (PublicSetup)
  • a cheating committer and prover with q hash queries in total make the verifier accept output tokens that are not the model's, at the weights that one extractor returns on the commitment and the committer's hash queries, with probability at most finalSoundnessError q, about q / 2^124 + 2^-101
theorem sound (setup : PublicSetup) : Sound (compile (flashProve setup)) finalSoundnessError
Not covered
  • finalSoundnessError q, about q / 2^124 + 2^-101, is a bound on the soundness error, not a security level.
  • Public files whose policy is not exact match (the verifier does not test whether it is); a provider that chooses its public files after seeing the hash function.
Remark

Soundness requires only FilesTaken (§4.4) and holds for every choice of honest provers and settings. This more general theorem has no card on this page (Johnson/Face/FinalSoundProof.lean:24; see the remark in §1); sound is proved by applying it to the setup's files. The public setup requires more because of the other theorems.

TheoremSoundness with bindingAtFullSide/Face/TheSixLines.lean:99–100
In words
In Lean · AtFullSide/Face/TheSixLines.lean, lines 99–100
Given

a public setup setup (PublicSetup)

theorem soundAndBinding (setup : PublicSetup) :
Then

soundness and binding, with the same extractor and bound for both: the soundness clause also holds with error finalBindingError q, and the commitment cannot be opened to weights other than the extractor's, except with probability finalBindingError q, about q / 2^124 + 2^-100, where q bounds the total number of hash queries of whoever made the commitment and of the prover (in the soundness clause) or the opener (in the binding clause)

SoundAndBinding (compile (flashProve setup)) finalBindingError
Not covered
  • An opening consists of weights and one number for the committer's randomness. This covers fewer openings than arbitrary coins would: nothing is said about an opening in which the salts of the first table's leaves (the first table: §4.3) have a different public prefix or length. For a small coinBound, binding would say almost nothing: at 0 there is only one choice of coins. For the honest provers and settings of the six theorems, the bound excludes none of the committer's choices of coins: coinBound + 1 is the committer's whole range, and for the files of a public setup every pair of an encoding randomness of the first table and a member of the list of its salts is given by a number at most coinBound (a theorem: AtFullSide/Face/FinalBindingOpeningsAtHonestProversAndSettingsOf.lean:39). No value is given for coinBound.
  • The statement does not say whose weights the extractor outputs.
  • Nothing is said about two openings to the same weights, or about several commitments.
  • The commitment is computed from the first table's Merkle root, its out-of-domain sample and part of what is read from the public files (§4.3); it does not cover the offline proof, the copies or their link proofs.
  • Public files whose policy is not exact match (the verifier does not test whether it is); a provider that chooses its public files after seeing the hash function.

The error function is existentially quantified, not a named function: the statement says that there is one and that it is at most finalZeroKnowledgeError within the stated limits on queries and replies; ZeroKnowledgeOn takes it as an argument.

Remark

The theorems on zero knowledge hold for up to 688,127 replies. Each reply, including a refused reply (the empty proof), is counted as one run of the online IOP; the statements contain only the count (the Lean comment says "is one run").

onlineRunsPerCopy is also the numeric literal 688,127, so (1) compares two literals. (2) relates that number to a table: 62 + 688,127 · 64 columns do not exceed a copy's 44,040,191.

(1) and (2) are conditions on numbers used in the proof of zero knowledge, which is why this theorem is one of the six. Copies are described in §6.4.

In the theorems on soundness, binding, completeness and zero knowledge, the hash function is sampled at random. The honest committer and prover are Lean definitions, not programs.

The Lean verifier:

In words
In Lean · AtFullSide/Face/TheSixLines.lean, lines 155–157
Given

def leanVerifier (setup : PublicSetup) :
Commitment → List Token → List Token → (compile (flashProve setup)).Proof → Bool :=
Value

the compiled verifier with each of its hash queries answered by blake2bHash, the hash function on bit strings built from BLAKE2b

Not covered
  • As a definition it cannot be run: parts of the verifier's term are defined by the axiom of choice, among them the one-to-one coding of its hash queries (lean/GAPS.md, 56).
  • The six theorems apply to a run only insofar as the run is proved to return this term's value. §5 describes what the command lean-verify runs and what is proved about it. In the Lean comment, "a second Lean text" means that executable form: a second implementation of the verifier in Lean.

As a definition, leanVerifier cannot be run: parts of the verifier's term are defined using the axiom of choice, including the injective encoding of its hash queries. We therefore provide a second, executable verifier written in Lean, executableVerifier, and prove its equality to leanVerifier.

TheoremThe executable verifier equals the Lean verifierAtFullSide/Face/ExecutableVerifierIsLeanVerifier.lean:47–50
In words
In Lean · AtFullSide/Face/ExecutableVerifierIsLeanVerifier.lean, lines 47–50
Given

a public setup (PublicSetup), a commitment, a prompt, output tokens and a parsed proof (FormBytes: five files from a parser outside Lean, and further tokens; elsewhere on this page: the proof as submitted)

theorem executableVerifier_eq_leanVerifier (setup : PublicSetup) (commitment : Commitment)
(prompt output : List Token) (proof : FlashProve.FormBytes) :
Then

on the setup's three public files and these inputs, executableVerifier returns a verdict (never none), and it equals that of leanVerifier

executableVerifier setup.files commitment prompt output proof =
some (leanVerifier setup commitment prompt output proof)
Not covered
  • The theorem applies only when the public files are those of a public setup (the argument setup.files). The command lean-verify does not enforce this: it does not reject public files that specify a policy other than exact match (A public setup).
  • The command lean-verify calls, one after another, the parts of the Lean function verdictOf. verdictOf parses the claim from the user's files (claimOf) and applies executableVerifier to it (verdictOf_eq_executableVerifier, proved by unfolding definitions). No theorem shows that claimOf implements the file format, and no theorem covers the parser outside Lean or the run itself. The other assumptions of a run are listed in Running the verifier.
Remark
  • This is an equation between values of deterministic Lean functions. It involves no random oracle and makes no security claim.
  • No theorem says that leanVerifier, executableVerifier or verdictOf is sound at BLAKE2b. Soundness is proved with the hash function sampled at random. That it carries over to leanVerifier at BLAKE2b is the Fiat–Shamir heuristic, an assumption.
  • Like leanVerifier, executableVerifier also uses the protocol's second, fixed hash function, which is not modelled as a random oracle (The second hash function).
  • The card of executableVerifier (§5) says what "executable" means.

What the theorems refer to

A public setup

A public setup consists of three public files (a parameter file, a layout file and a scale file) that satisfy four conditions (FilesInUse, §4.4):

  • They are in the verifier's scope. The layout file is the layout file of the stored full-size example. The parameter file agrees byte for byte with that example's parameter file, except for eight numbers: five numbers of the normalizations and the three numbers of the acceptance policy. The third condition below fixes the three policy numbers, so only the five numbers of the normalizations are free in the parameter file.
  • They parse without error.
  • They specify the exact-match policy: every output token must be the model's own choice (greedy decoding). The verifier does not check this condition.
  • They pass the test protocolDataWellFormed, which the verifier also performs: the protocol's data can be built from them without error, no list of rounds is empty, the data for the key and for the proof have the full-size depth, and the sizes lie within fixed limits.

The library defines one public setup, storedSetup (§4.4), as a Lean term. No theorem relates it to a file on disk; a program outside Lean compares it with the files of the shipped example.

Three definitions that the theorems use. A fourth, onlineRunsPerCopy, is in §6.4.

DefinitionThe public setup: three public filesAtFullSide/Face/TheSixLines.lean:69–75
In words
In Lean · AtFullSide/Face/TheSixLines.lean, lines 69–75

Three public files that a user has in addition to the commitment, fixed before the hash function is sampled. They determine the model shape and the instance of the protocol; only the scale file and five numbers of the parameter file (parameters of the normalizations) are free.

structure PublicSetup where
Files

files: the parameter file, the layout file and the scale file

/-- The three public files. -/
files : PublicFiles

readParameters: what reading the files returns

/-- What the reader returns at them. -/
readParameters : Inst.Model.ScalesAndPolicy
Condition

the field inUse requires (FilesInUse, §4.4):

  • that the verifier takes them
  • that reading them returns readParameters
  • that their policy is exact match
  • that they pass the test protocolDataWellFormed: the protocol's data can be built from them without error, no list of rounds is empty, the data for the key and for the proof have the full-size depth, and the sizes are within fixed limits; the test is treated as a black box on this page
/-- They are in scope, read so, state exact match and pass the test. -/
inUse : FilesInUse files readParameters
Not covered

The files are not the PublicParameters of an argument system (§1), which compile sets to Unit. What the files reveal about the weights (a fitted model's scale file is derived from its weights) is not covered by the theorems on zero knowledge (§6.3).

For some valid choices of the quantization scales, the outputs of the value and up projections are all zero, so no layer changes the residual stream (checked by hand, not proved: the head of Cm/Rel2Idle.lean, on sIdle, to which the comment on weightsAreValid in VerifiableInference/ModelWeights.lean points); for public files that state such settings the theorems say little. A reader has to inspect the scale file.

Remark

storedSetup (below) is the only public setup that the library exhibits. That its files form a public setup is a theorem (filesInUse_stored). Its scale file is that of an example with synthetic weights (according to the head comment of Ladder/Stored.lean; no theorem).

Whoever commits writes the scale file.

DefinitionFlashProve at a public setup: the input to compileAtFullSide/Face/TheSixLines.lean:82–84
In words
In Lean · AtFullSide/Face/TheSixLines.lean, lines 82–84

The input to compile: not a bare interactive oracle proof, but a record that contains the protocol with its layout into hash queries. There is one for each public setup: FlashProve is a family of protocols.

The protocol uses a second hash function, secondHashFunction, a fixed function that is not modelled as a random oracle (§5).

def flashProve (setup : PublicSetup) : Compilable :=
Value

flashProveAtFiles (§4.4) with its three arguments determined by the public setup:

  • the files
  • the model's settings read from them
flashProveAtFiles setup.files (settingsOfRead setup.readParameters)
  • the honest provers and settings
(honestProversAndSettings setup.files (settingsOfRead setup.readParameters))
Remark

The protocol is a linkable holographic IOP (§3):

  • an encoder and a decoder for the index (here: made from the weights)
  • an out-of-domain sample on each encoding
  • three IOPs, each meant to prove one statement:
    • offline: one encoding decodes
    • link: two encodings decode to the same index
    • online: a request's claim holds of the index that an encoding decodes to

Holographic IOPs and their compilation are defined in Fractal, ePrint 2019/1076 (§3).

DefinitionThe honest provers and settings, as a closed termAtFullSide/Face/HonestProversAndSettingsValue.lean:32
In words
In Lean · AtFullSide/Face/HonestProversAndSettingsValue.lean, lines 32–32

The honest provers and settings of the six theorems: a single closed term that gives, for every choice of public files and settings:

  • the three honest IOP provers
  • the honest committer's and prover's settings: what they choose in addition to the provers, including the public prefixes of their salts, how long a search for a nonce may run, and a fall-back instance

It contains no committer: compile constructs the honest committer.

It is a definition, not a program: it obtains the model's trace by a non-constructive choice.

The verifier reads none of it.

noncomputable def honestProversAndSettings : HonestProversAndSettings := honestProversAndSettingsOf thePartsAt
Not covered

A black box on this page: it depends on about 16,000 named declarations of this library, of which the page shows about five hundred.

Remark

The provers consist of parts (in Lean: senders), one for each step of the protocol. Where a function called by such a part refuses, the part sends a fixed default value and does not stop.

  • There are some two dozen such places, listed in E2E/TheHonestProverStatements.lean, section 3.
  • The statements are about the provers as defined, including these default values; it is not shown that they are never used.

The numbers in these theorems:

  • finalSoundnessError q = 16 (q + 1 + 2^23) / 2^128 + (q + 2^23 + 3)^2 / 2^256, about q / 2^124 + 2^-101
  • finalBindingError q: about q / 2^124 + 2^-100
  • finalCompletenessError = 2^-40
  • finalZeroKnowledgeError = 2^-154
  • finalVerifierQueries = 2^64
  • finalReplyCount = 688,127
  • honestQueryBudget = 2^48

§4.4 specifies whose hash queries q counts.

1. Soundness

  • A committer outputs a commitment of 256 bits. The commitment, together with the committer's queries to the hash function and their answers, determines at most one choice of weights: a fixed extractor, a function that is not shown to be computable, outputs it from these.
  • Let t₁ bound the committer's queries, and consider any prover that runs afterwards and makes at most t₂ queries. Except with probability at most ε(t₁ + t₂), over the hash function and the random choices of the committer and the prover, the output tokens that the verifier accepts are the output of the model with these weights on the prompt. This bounds the probability of a false accept, not the conditional probability that an accepted output is false.
  • By a separate clause (§1.1), an opener with at most t₂ queries outputs an opening to other weights with probability at most ε(t₁ + t₂). The same weights can have many commitments, because the honest committer computes the commitment from the weights and its own randomness.

Randomized and deterministic algorithms, queries to the hash function, query logs and probabilities are those of the random oracle model (§8).

The theorem sound. For every public setup, the compiled argument system compile (flashProve setup), with the model settings read from the public files, satisfies Sound (above) with the error function finalSoundnessError.

Expanded. There is an extractor such that, for every committer with at most t₁ queries to the random oracle and every prover with at most t₂ queries, the following event has probability at most finalSoundnessError (t₁ + t₂): the verifier accepts output tokens that are not the model's output with the weights that the extractor outputs, given the commitment and the committer's queries.

  • The probability is taken over the random oracle and the coins of the two adversaries.
  • The prover chooses the prompt and the output tokens, and the committer passes its state to the prover.
  • If the extractor outputs no weights, every accepted proof counts toward this event.

Remark. The proof of sound uses sound_of_verify_at (Johnson/Goal/Skeleton/SoundOfVerifyAt.lean:69), the soundness theorem for verify, FlashProve's verifier. Its three hypotheses are the fields of FilesTaken. Soundness of compile at flashProveAtFiles follows from sound_of_verify_at for arbitrary honest provers and settings (Johnson/Face/FinalSoundProof.lean:24).

1.1 With a binding commitment

SoundAndBinding has a second clause, on openings of the commitment. An opening of a commitment to given weights is a pair of these weights and commitment randomness on which commit returns that commitment. The clause states the following. For every committer with at most committerQueries queries, and every opener with at most proverQueries queries that is given the committer's state, the probability that the opener outputs an opening of the committer's commitment to weights that the extractor does not output is at most ε(committerQueries + proverQueries).

SoundOpened is a statement without an extractor. SoundAndBinding with error ε implies SoundOpened with error 2 ε. The library proves SoundOpened for the compiled system, for public files that satisfy FilesInUse, with the bound 2 · finalBindingError (finalSoundOpened_value, AtFullSide/Face/FinalBindingAtTheValue.lean; no card on this page).

2. The model

The model is a single function, the field nextToken of the argument system (§1).

  • Its inputs are weights and a list of tokens. The quantization parameters are fields of the model settings (Appendix C), and the model settings are not part of the weights.
  • It returns the next token, or nothing if the model is undefined on these tokens.
  • It does not query the hash function and uses no randomness.
  • The soundness statements refer to it only through IsModelOutput (§1).

FlashProve's model is defined in Appendix C.

3. The protocol

The verifier is compiled from a protocol, a linkable holographic IOP, which does not query the random oracle. Such a protocol has an encoder with a decoder, an out-of-domain sample on each encoding, and three interactive oracle proofs (IOPs): offline, link and online. The general definition follows; FlashProve's protocol is defined in Appendix A.

Credits, among them the paper that this protocol builds on: lean/CREDITS.md. The idea is public: holographic IOPs and their compilation to arguments in the random oracle model are defined in A. Chiesa, D. Ojha, N. Spooner, "Fractal: Post-Quantum and Transparent Recursive Proofs from Holography", ePrint 2019/1076 (eprint.iacr.org/2019/1076). This page's design, and its paragraph "Checking the proofs yourself", are modelled on veil.succinct.xyz (Succinct).

4. The compiler

This section presents the library's compiler. It consists of an inner and an outer compiler (§4.3).

The inner compiler. It is defined for every input of type InnerCompilerInput. Such an input consists of any protocol of type HolographicProtocol (§3) and further data written by hand for that protocol, including the layout of its rounds and openings in hash queries. innerSystem constructs an argument system from such an input, and innerCompiledVerifier is the verifier of that system.

The outer compiler, compile. It is defined for every input of type Compilable. Its verifier performs a test on the public files, parses the proof (the field parse of the proof format, §4.3), performs two readings of the public files (queries to the hash function at strings computed from them), and then runs innerCompiledVerifier. Its committer and prover are constructed from the honest provers in its input. compile is not a compiler for arbitrary IOPs: some fields of its input follow FlashProve's format, namely the two readings of the public files, a test on a first hash block, and the proof format.

The Lean code has three layers, listed here from the bottom up:

  • What is hashed (§4.1). The compiled verifier queries separate oracles, one for each purpose. They are implemented by the single random oracle, with domain separation. Each oracle string is replaced by Merkle roots.
  • The BCS transformation for one IOP (§4.2). The verifier's challenges are computed from answers of a Fiat–Shamir oracle, and the positions that the IOP's verifier reads are opened against the roots.
  • The whole verifier and the argument system (§4.3).

The outer compiler constructs the committer and the prover from the honest IOP provers in its input, whereas the inner compiler takes the committer and the prover as fields of its input. As a result, the protocol's structure (§3) and the compiler's input (§4.3) have fields, such as honest provers, that are not used to construct the compiled system; see the remark in §6.4.

The definitions of the compiler's verifier. These definitions are written for any protocol of the library's type (§3).

  • compiledVerifier first performs a scope test on the public files. It then performs three steps that depend on FlashProve's files and proof format: one parses the proof and two read the public files. It calls innerCompiledVerifier.
  • innerCompiledVerifier runs the next three definitions.
  • Arg.buildInstance rejects if no instance can be built from the request.
  • verifyDigestKey checks that the commitment equals the hash function's value at the encoding of the key in the proof (§4.3).
  • verifyAtKeyRoot builds the whole key from the proof and calls verifyAtFullKey.
  • verifyAtFullKey performs six checks: the number of the copy (§6.4), two seeds, and the verifiers of the three IOPs (offline, link, online).
  • verifyOneProtocol is the verifier of one IOP. Each of the last three checks of verifyAtFullKey calls it. The definitions that it calls have their own cards below it in §4.2.

4.1 What is hashed, and Merkle trees

This subsection shows how the compiled algorithms use the single hash function. None of its definitions mentions FlashProve. HashLayout is stated for any protocol of type HolographicProtocol (§3). typedOracleFamily, Check and hashTreeNode are stated for the batch protocol with a leaf body that typedOracleCarrier constructs from such a protocol. OracleCoding is stated for any family of oracles, and Opening for any alphabet.

4.2 The BCS transformation: one IOP, verified with the hash function

The BCS transformation makes one IOP non-interactive. Each of the prover's oracle strings is replaced by the root of a Merkle tree. Each challenge of the verifier is computed from an answer of a Fiat–Shamir oracle, queried on what was fixed before that challenge.

One definition is used for all three IOPs of the protocol (§3).

verifyOneProtocol does not constrain three things (see "Limits" at the head of its Lean file):

  • an accepted proof string remains accepted after any change to its field for the part sent in the clear of a component not sent in its round, and, if the chain has no first shared round, to rtreq (any digest) and slot (any number below 2^depthReq)
  • the root of a component under which the IOP's verifier opens nothing; it is not checked against anything, and it is a field of a query of its round: the Fiat–Shamir query or, for the batch position's root in the first shared round, the query to the oracle g, whose answer is the batch position's value (recomputeChain)
  • the digests in Merkle paths that the joint verification does not use (§4.2, under Merkle paths)

It is not proved that no other change turns an accepted proof string into another accepted one.

Not covered
  • The two tests on openings range over the positions listed by the query layout (posAt0, posAtJ, ext.all). They cover every position if the layout is well-formed (WireRB.OKG, WireE.OK), which the theorems that use them assume.
  • If the chain has passed the first shared round, the length of rsalt is not tested, and no part of rsalt is compared with the field slot. Nevertheless, rsalt is not free to change: a different rsalt gives a different input of the leaf's hash (by reading; no theorem).
Remark

Remark

forestsOf lists the openings to verify (Check, §4.1), at positions that the IOP's verifier reads:

  • in the prover's oracle strings (read at x, ρ and the parts sent in the clear): at every read position of a leaf, in each tree that has a depth and a root. Nothing more is checked where the depths or the roots end (the component is not sent, or has no further tree)
  • in the external oracle strings (read at x and ρ): at every read position listed in wq, against the entry of cms that the layout specifies (a default digest if cms has none)

Where the layout's pruning flag (pr0, prJ, pr) is set, the opened leaves are verified together; elsewhere each opening is verified along its own path.

afterF accepts if all three hold:

  • reqPart: if the last phase contains a batch position's value c, the check in the Merkle tree over the batch (reqCheck) passes: π.path has length depthReq, π.slot is less than 2^depthReq, and hashing from the leaf (the hash of c followed by π.rsalt) up the path gives π.rtreq; if the last phase contains no such value, this condition holds

verifyOneProtocol calls three definitions, each with a card above:

  • recomputeChainOfProof, which calls recomputeChain on the parts of the proof string;
  • proofHasStrictFormat, which checks the format;
  • checkPrunedOpenings, which checks the openings, performs the check in the tree over the batch, and evaluates the IOP verifier's own decision.

checkPrunedOpenings calls forestsOf and afterF, each with a card above. Thus, in the Lean code on this page, a challenge can be traced from what is hashed to its value, then to the positions that the IOP's verifier reads for it (Q.loc.reads, Q.loc.extReads), and into the IOP verifier's decision (Q.loc.accept, at the transcript constructed by mkTr). Of the definitions that these three, forestsOf and afterF call in turn, recomputeChain has a card above. The others (including forestsB, forestExt, runForests, reqPart, mkTr, effPlains, strictSB, strictExt) have no card on this page. The Lean code of these eight is in §9.

Merkle paths. The Merkle path of each opening must have length equal to the depth of its tree. The joint verification reads only those digests in these paths that it needs: where two opened nodes are siblings, it reads the digest of neither. The other digests are not checked against anything. Neither proofHasStrictFormat nor checkPrunedOpenings rejects them, so a typed proof can be altered at these places and still be accepted. This is malleability of the proof string, not a gap in soundness: the bound of sound holds for arbitrary values of these entries (lean/GAPS.md, 14 and 66).

The structure used by verifyOneProtocol. verifyOneProtocol is stated for a smaller structure, which typedOracleCarrier constructs from a protocol of type HolographicProtocol. It keeps the protocol's shapes and types, but not its index or its provers. That structure has no card on this page either.

4.3 The verifier, and the compiled argument system

compile takes one record, Compilable. Its main fields are the public side (the protocol, its hash layout, two readings of the public files, and the model), the honest provers with their settings, and the format in which a proof is written.

It returns an argument system. The verifier of that system depends only on the public side and on the parser of the proof format.

The six theorems concern only compile at flashProveAtFiles.

Remark

The system has no public parameters.

The committer:

  • encodes the index of the weights as a first table and as furtherCopies + 1 copies of it
  • builds a salted Merkle tree over each table, with its out-of-domain sample
  • adds the offline proof for the first table and a link proof for each copy
  • returns a commitment of 256 bits

The prover keeps no state:

  • it runs the committer again on the same randomness
  • then proves one request on one copy, sampled at random, using the online proof

How an input becomes an argument system · 8 cards

The definitions in this folded section have at most a few lines each. They pass arguments from innerCompiledVerifier to Arg.buildInstance, verifyDigestKey and verifyAtKeyRoot. schemeOverOneHashFunction (above) does more: it implements the separate oracles of verifyAtKeyRoot by the single hash function (§4.1). ArgumentSystem.ofArgument presents the result as an argument system.

In Lean · Johnson/Face/Compiler.lean, lines 314–318

The four parts of an argument system that its verifier does not read.

structure CompiledSide (Weights Form : Type) where
Randomness : Type
sample : RandomizedAlgorithm Randomness
commit : Weights → Randomness → DeterministicAlgorithm Commitment
prove : Weights → Randomness → List Token → List Token → RandomizedAlgorithm Form

The honest committer stores the weights as an encoded table, the first table, and answers requests from further encodings of it, called copies. Each copy has a link proof, which is meant to show that the copy decodes to the same index as the first table. The number of copies is a setting in honestProversAndSettings, which produces one copy (furtherCopies = 0).

The committer encodes the index as the first table, hashes that table into a Merkle tree, computes its out-of-domain sample and adds the offline proof. Each copy gets a link proof. The commitment has 256 bits. It is the hash function's answer on one bit string, the encoding of the key. The field keyCode of the hash layout computes this string from the key (the first table's Merkle root and its out-of-domain sample) and a part of what is read from the public files. The compiler does not fix which part. For FlashProve it is the digest of the files; this was found by reading the Lean code and is not stated by any theorem (lean/GAPS.md, 5).

The verifier takes the first table's root and out-of-domain sample from the proof, computes the same bit string, and compares the hash function's answer on it with the commitment.

It then recomputes the out-of-domain seeds of the first table and of the copy that the proof uses, and runs the compiled verifiers of the three IOPs: offline on the first table's root, link on both roots, and online on the copy's root and the request. Finally, it applies a test supplied by the hash layout (num) to the number that the proof gives for that copy and to the parts of the online proof that are sent in the clear. The compiler assumes nothing about this test.

Some rounds require proof of work. The prover must find a nonce for which the round's Fiat–Shamir answer passes a test on some of its bits, and the verifier rejects otherwise. In FlashProve's IOPs these bits are further bits of the round's challenge, and the IOP's verifier rejects unless all of them are 0 (Appendix A, The terms of this appendix, proof-of-work bits). The search for a nonce is called proof-of-work grinding; each failed attempt costs one hash query.

4.4 FlashProve

This section applies the compiler to one input, flashProveAtFiles, and states what is required of the result. compile (flashProve setup) is the compiled argument system: a committer, a prover and a verifier that query a random oracle. The six theorems (Final statements) are about compile at this input only.

finalSoundnessError q = 16 (q + 1 + 2^23) / 2^128 + (q + 2^23 + 3)^2 / 2^256. Here q counts the hash queries of the committer and the prover together, honest or adversarial (in sound, adversarial). finalBindingError is defined below, among the values substituted for the parameters. finalCompletenessError is 2^-40.

(honest : HonestProversAndSettingsAtFiles files settings) :
(compile (flashProveAtFiles files settings honest)).verify = finalVerifier files settings
Remark

Hence the verifier does not depend on the honest provers and settings.

((errorFactorPerQuery * (t + verifierQueryAllowance) : ℕ) : ℝ≥0∞) * (2 : ℝ≥0∞)⁻¹ ^ 128 +

Remark

At t = 0 this error is about 2^-101, and finalBindingError, the maximum of it and a soundness term, is about 2^-100.

The experiment in the second clause of SoundAndBinding runs the honest committer once more. That run's queries are not the adversary's; honestBudget accounts for them in the square term.

The bad event that such a run can cause is that one of its answers equals another answer or a value that the adversary wrote. A bound on only these events has the form 3 · (t + 2 q + 2)² / 2^256, where q bounds the queries of one run of the committer.

Wherever this error is less than 1, that bound is smaller than it because of the linear term, not the square term; without the linear term, the square term would have to take that form.

The linear term may also have to account for events that a committer can search for, such as a collision at a seed.

5. The explicit hash function

In the theorems on soundness, binding, completeness and zero knowledge, the hash function is sampled uniformly at random, so these are statements in the random oracle model. compile does not take the hash function as a parameter. A program uses one concrete hash function instead. leanVerifier uses blake2bHash, a function from bit strings to 256 bits built from BLAKE2b (Appendix B), in place of the random oracle.

The verifier instantiated with BLAKE2b
  • leanVerifier is the verifier of §4.3 with each of its queries answered by blake2bHash. finalVerifierProgram is defined for arbitrary public files, using only the public part of the compiler's input. At the files of a public setup it equals leanVerifier (leanVerifier_eq, below).
  • The argument form of leanVerifier is what this page calls the proof as submitted: a list of tokens and five byte strings. It is not the file that the prover writes. A program outside Lean splits the prover's files into the five byte strings. The tokens are the tokens of the request that follow the checked positions; they are read from the request file (formOf, Johnson/PVR/Program.lean:113).
  • verdictOf (card below) reads eleven files: the three public files; the user's three files, from which the commitment, the prompt and the output are parsed; and five parsed files, which are the five byte strings of form.
  • verdictOf uses its own definitions of several objects. This page names three of them:
    • the order of the steps (fastSteps, Johnson/Top/Fire/Code/VerifyVFastStepsD.lean:103);
    • the verifier of one file (verifyWholeX, OnBytes/Maker/LessWhole.lean:158; for the link, stagesWL, Johnson/RunOne/StrictLinkWL.lean:68);
    • how a typed query is answered from the hash function on bytes (famFQ, Johnson/PV/MFullQ.lean:55).
The Fiat–Shamir heuristic

The heuristic is the assumption that, in the theorems on soundness, binding, completeness and zero knowledge, blake2bHash may be treated as a function sampled uniformly at random (the random oracle model). For zero knowledge, the simulator also answers the hash queries in place of this function (§8). The heuristic is not a theorem and is not stated in Lean. It is an assumption about the hash function and this argument system together. It also carries one assumption about the second hash function: that blake2bHash behaves like a random function that is independent of it (below).

The second hash function

The IOP being compiled itself uses a second hash function, secondHashFunction. It is a fixed function, built from BLAKE2b's compression function with a number written into the block counter. It is part of FlashProve's description (Appendix A); the six theorems do not take it as a parameter. It is therefore part of the compiled verifier, and hence of leanVerifier.

  • Where it is used. According to the comments in the Lean code, it is applied, among other places, to the public files when the protocol's public part is computed, and to the request in the verifier's tests on the instance. It has other uses, not all of which are listed on this page. For example, the test protocolDataWellFormed, the extractor and the honest online prover are defined using it. Through protocolDataWellFormed it also appears in the hypothesis of the six theorems.
  • How the theorems treat it. It is not modelled as a random oracle: the theorems on soundness, binding, completeness and zero knowledge sample one hash function and keep this one fixed. They assume no property of it, not even collision resistance. They are proved for this one function. A soundness statement for an arbitrary function in its place (G7', Ladder.lean) is stated in the library but not proved. Each theorem holds for every request in its scope, and hence also for a request in that scope that an adversary chooses knowing this function.
  • What the heuristic assumes about it. In the theorems, queries to this function are not queries to the sampled function, and the sampled function is independent of it. The heuristic replaces the sampled function by blake2bHash, which is built from the same compression function. It therefore also assumes that blake2bHash behaves like a random function that is independent of the second hash function. This assumption is made outside Lean and is not a hypothesis of any theorem (lean/LIMITS.md, Assumption 2, second half).

Running the verifier

The command lean-verify evaluates the Lean function run, an IO wrapper that calls the three parts of verdictOf in turn (claimOf, stepsOf, verdictAt), with BLAKE2b as the hash function. The theorem verdictOf_at shows that these three parts compose to verdictOf. verdictOf parses the claim from the user's files and applies executableVerifier to it (verdictOf_eq_executableVerifier). The function verdictOf is a second implementation of the verifier in Lean. It uses the same definitions of the protocol's data and decisions, and has steps of its own (§5).

What is proved

The eight theorems of this list (executableVerifier_eq_leanVerifier, executableVerifier_eq_leanVerifier_stored, verdictOf_eq_executableVerifier, verdictOf_eq_leanVerifier, verdictOf_eq_finalVerifierProgram, leanVerifier_eq, verdictOf_map, verdictOf_none) are equations between values of deterministic Lean functions. None of them involves a random oracle or makes a security claim.

  • executableVerifier_eq_leanVerifier (Final statements): for every public setup, executableVerifier applied to the setup's public files returns the verdict of leanVerifier. executableVerifier_eq_leanVerifier_stored (no card on this page) is its instance at the stored public files.
  • verdictOf_eq_executableVerifier (card above): verdictOf parses the claim from the user's files and applies executableVerifier to the public files, the claim and the parsed proof. It is proved by unfolding definitions.
  • verdictOf_eq_leanVerifier (card above): the same fact as the first, stated for verdictOf. It therefore has two further hypotheses: the claim can be parsed, and the public files are those of the setup.
  • verdictOf_eq_finalVerifierProgram and leanVerifier_eq (cards above) relate verdictOf and leanVerifier to a common term, finalVerifierProgram (the compiled verifier evaluated with blake2bHash on given public files).
  • The theorem verdictOf_map (Johnson/PVR/ProgramTotal.lean; no card on this page). For arbitrary public files, whenever the commitment, the prompt and the output can be parsed from the user's files, verdictOf returns the verdict of VerifierAndGoals.verify (Ladder.lean; no card on this page) for FlashProve's description (flashProveDescription), which includes the second hash function, evaluated with BLAKE2b. VerifierAndGoals.verify is the verifier in the soundness theorem sound_of_verify_at, whose hypotheses are that the public files are in scope, parse, and specify exact match. It equals the compiled system's verify by compile_flashProve_verify_eq and theDescription_eq.
  • If the commitment, the prompt or the output cannot be parsed, verdictOf returns no verdict (verdictOf_none).

The agreement is not special to BLAKE2b: for every function O from byte strings to 32-byte strings, the executable form run with O returns the verdict of VerifierAndGoals.verify evaluated with hashOf O (PV.Ride.verdictThe_eq, Johnson/PVR/RideEveryHash.lean:116). Hence its decision satisfies SoundOfDecision, a restatement of Sound, with a sampled hash function, under the hypotheses and the bound of sound_of_verify_at (PV.Ride.sound_of_the_form_events_oOf, Johnson/PVR/SoundOfTheFormEvents.lean:264). Neither theorem has a card on this page, and neither gives soundness at the concrete hash function.

The security statements for the compiled system are stated with the hash function sampled at random. Soundness at BLAKE2b is therefore not a theorem (see the card executableVerifier_eq_leanVerifier, Final statements).

What is not proved
  • These theorems concern the Lean functions verdictOf, executableVerifier, finalVerifierProgram and leanVerifier, not the run of the command lean-verify. No theorem is about the command itself, which consists of a script, an IO wrapper in Lean (run), natively compiled helper code, and Lean's compiler, interpreter and runtime.
  • executableVerifier, and hence verdictOf, does not check every condition of a public setup. It tests that the public files are in the verifier's scope, can be read and are well formed; it does not check that they specify the exact-match policy. If the public files pass the scope test (InScope) but specify another policy, the verifier may accept, and sound does not apply. The serving scripts use such a policy, the tolerant policy.
  • The theorems on soundness, binding, completeness and zero knowledge are stated for a hash function sampled uniformly at random, whereas leanVerifier fixes it to blake2bHash. Hence no theorem bounds the probability that leanVerifier accepts a false claim, and no theorem shows that it accepts even one honest proof.
What is trusted, and where files are parsed
  • The script lean_verify.sh, the IO wrapper run, the natively compiled helper code, and Lean's compiler, interpreter and runtime are trusted.
  • A parser outside Lean, which is not verified, splits the prover's files into the five byte strings of the proof as submitted. For soundness, its output is treated as chosen by the prover: a wrongly parsed file can cause an honest proof to be rejected, but it gives a prover no additional power. Hence soundness does not depend on the parser; only the acceptance of honest proofs does.
  • The Lean function claimOf, with the functions that it calls, parses the user's three files into the commitment, the prompt, the output and the remaining tokens of the request. The first three form the claim, and the last is passed to the verifier as part of the proof. No theorem shows that claimOf implements the file format (lean/GAPS.md, 37).
  • The verifier's own parser, the field parse of the proof format (§4.3), is defined in Lean and maps the prompt, the output and the proof as submitted to a typed proof. The verifier calls it, so it is covered by sound.
What was run

These are tests, not theorems. All used synthetic weights. One Lean file, with one definition and four theorems, which nothing else imports, was added after the runs reported here and checked on its own (lean/CHECK-RESULTS.md). The runs executed the parts of verdictOf, not executableVerifier under that name.

  • With this repository's Lean files, the command accepted all 88 honest proofs. Of these, 86 used the exact-match policy and the stored setup's three public files, which were identified by checksums compared outside Lean; 2 used the tolerant policy. All 88 had been run before. None of them is known to have been generated by this repository's prover, and 3 were generated by test programs.
  • With this repository's Lean files, none of 71 invalid inputs (57 false proofs, 5 honest proofs paired with a false claim, 9 altered parameter files) was accepted: the Lean part of the command rejected 59, and the parser stopped 12 before they reached it.
  • One newly generated proof, which according to its builders was produced by this repository's prover, was also accepted, with the exact-match policy. It ran in a directory whose compiled files matched this repository's build before and after an earlier run; they were not checksummed after this run.
  • In a separate run, with Lean files that differ from this repository's and with the parsed files passed directly to the executable form, 17 proof files were altered without changing a true claim. Of these, 9 were accepted; for 2 of these 9 a rejection had been expected (lean/THEOREM.md, "Altered proof files that leave the claim untouched were accepted"; §11).
  • In none of these runs was a claim accepted that was false under the policy of its own public files.

6. The provider's side

For a provider who cares that the weights stay hidden. Three things to read:

  • the statement: ZeroKnowledgeOn (§6.3), with its two experiments (§6.2)
  • what is not hidden: one bit for each request (requestOutcome: served or refused, §6.1), and what the three public files reveal about the weights, which none of the six theorems covers, nor zeroKnowledgeAtEveryRequest (§6.3)
  • the two theorems zeroKnowledgeOnCanServe and refusedHandsOutNoProof, and what follows from them for every request (§6.3). They concern the honest committer and prover as Lean definitions, which compile constructs from honestProversAndSettings (a black box on this page). Nothing is proved about the programs.

Completeness and zero knowledge are statements about the honest committer and the honest prover. A reader who relies on proofs does not need them; the provider does.

Completeness and zero knowledge are stated for one commitment by the honest committer and one request per proof, with the prover's own coins fresh and uniform for each reply. In the completeness theorem the weights and the request are fixed before the hash function is sampled; a request chosen after seeing the commitment or the hash function is not covered. With honestProversAndSettings the committer makes one copy of the committed table (on copies, see §6.4). The theorems of this section say nothing about an honest committer that makes more copies.

6.1 Completeness

  • For one commitment and one request that can be served and whose output tokens are the model's, the honest proof is accepted, except with probability at most 2^-40.

A request can be served (CanServe) if its tokens are in the vocabulary, its output is not empty, and the model has a value on the whole window of 1,024 tokens. The completeness theorem says nothing about a request that cannot be served or whose output is not the model's. No theorem states that a request is served at a real model's weights (see the folded section below that begins Notes: two definitions).

The theorem completeOnCanServe, in full. For every public setup, compile (flashProve setup) satisfies CompleteOn (above) with CanServe and finalCompletenessError. That is:

  • for all weights and every request that can be served and whose output tokens are the model's,
  • when the honest committer commits and the honest prover proves,
  • the verifier rejects with probability at most 2^-40, over the random oracle and the coins of the honest committer and prover.

Remark. The library proves it equivalent to a second form, stated for well-formed requests whose result is the claimed output (finalComplete_iff_completeOn, Johnson/Face/Checks.lean:57); both terms are defined below.

Where the theorem says nothing. The theorem completeOnCanServe says nothing about a request whose result is none or tokens other than the claimed ones. For such a request requestOutcome is refused, and refusedHandsOutNoProof states that the prover's reply is the empty proof (noProofForm: a form all of whose parts are empty). None of the six theorems states that a refusal can be checked.

A well-formed request. A request (a prompt with a claimed output) is well formed (RequestForm) if every token is in the vocabulary, neither list is empty, and the two together have at most 1,025 tokens.

The model's result (requestResult, Appendix C) is obtained from one run of the model on a window of exactly 1,024 tokens: the prompt, the claimed output, then token 0 as often as needed, all truncated to 1,024 tokens (IntegerModel.zeroFilledWindow). If the request has 1,025 tokens, the last output token is outside the window: the run does not read it, and it is only compared with the run's choice at the window's last position.

  • The result is none if the model has no value on that window, including the padded positions.
  • Otherwise it is some of the tokens that the run chooses at the positions just before the output tokens.

The bit. requestOutcome assigns each request one of two values, served or refused. A request is refused if it is ill-formed, if the model has no result on it, or if the result differs from the claimed output. The bit depends on the weights and is not hidden: zeroKnowledgeAtEveryRequest gives it to the simulator. In that statement each reply shows the verifier nothing in addition to a proof.

At valid settings, a request is served if and only if it can be served and its output tokens are the model's (served_iff_canServe, VerifiableInference/AtEveryRequestGuards.lean:127).

The theorem refusedHandsOutNoProof, in full. The theorem concerns the output of the compiled prover. For every public setup,

  • for all weights, all commitment randomness, every request whose requestOutcome is refused, well-formed or not, and every hash function,
  • each reply that the prover returns with non-zero probability is the empty proof (noProofForm: a form all of whose parts are empty).

Not covered. A refusal is not checked: an empty proof proves nothing, and a prover can return it for a request that it could serve.

Remarks.

  • The condition is on every possible reply, so it has no error term.
  • The compiled verifier rejects the empty proof for every hash function and every public setup (rejectsEmptyProof).
  • The converse is not claimed: the reply to a served request can also be the empty proof. Among other cases, this happens when a search for a proof-of-work nonce (§4.3) fails, and when the compiled prover withholds a proof string because the run's verifier messages are in one of the honest provers' abort sets (Appendix A); one part of the online prover's abort set depends on its private input. The reply is empty if any of the three proof strings (offline, link, online) is missing. The simulator of zeroKnowledgeAtEveryRequest simulates a failed nonce search. It does not simulate the aborts that depend on the online prover's private input; their probability, at most 2^-174 for each reply, is counted in the bound 2^-154 (§4.4). In each of these cases the reply looks like the reply to a refused request.
  • refusedHandsOutNoProof is proved more generally, for public files that meet FilesTaken: finalRefusedHandsOutNoProof_value (AtFullSide/Face/TheFinalStatementOneBitHolds.lean:60).

Notes: two definitions of "the model's output" · that the statement is not vacuous · 2 cards

Two definitions of "the model's output".

  • Soundness, CompleteOn and ZeroKnowledgeOn use IsModelOutput (§1), which runs the model on the prompt followed by each proper prefix of the output, without padding.
  • requestOutcome uses the model's result, computed by one run on the padded window; CanServe requires that this run has a value.

One direction is proved. At the settings given by public files (these settings pass settingsAreValid, the library's test on sizes and quantization ranges), if a request is well formed and its result is the claimed output, then each output token is the model's next token in the sense of §1 (from wellFormed_and_result_iff, VerifiableInference/WellFormedRequests.lean:48).

The other direction fails for the empty output, which is the model's in the sense of §1, while a request with empty output is not well formed. It may also fail for a well-formed request if the model has no value at the last output token's position or at a padded position: such a request would be refused although its output is the model's in the sense of §1. No theorem rules this out, except for weights that meet a condition stated in the library but not on this page. No example of this is proved.

Not vacuous. For every set of public files that meets FilesInUse (one exists: filesInUse_stored), some request is served at some weights (someRequestIsServedInUse, below). Those weights are artificial: all their layers are zero. No theorem states that a request is served at a real model's weights, and at the settings that the stored public files give there are weights at which no request can be served (canServe_nowhere_atHaltingWeights, above).

6.2 The two experiments of zero knowledge

A malicious verifier is given the commitment and then proofs. The request for each proof is picked by a chooser: a function that maps the verifier's view so far to a request, or to nothing, in which case the experiment ends. In the real experiment, the hash function is sampled uniformly at random, and the honest committer and the honest prover run. In the simulated experiment, the simulator replaces all three; it is given each request and the information about the weights that the statement specifies.

This page has two definitions of a simulator, each with its own simulated experiment; the real experiment is the same for both.

  • Simulator is the general one: for each request it is given only the request. ZeroKnowledgeOn is stated with it.
  • AtEveryRequest.Simulator takes one more argument: the information it is given about each request. ZeroKnowledgeWhere, and hence the theorem zeroKnowledgeAtEveryRequest, is stated in terms of it. Its card is in a folded section in §6.3.

6.3 Zero knowledge

  • One simulator, fixed before the weights, produces the commitment, the replies and the hash answers. It may depend on the public files; it gets each request and the largest number of replies, and nothing about the weights.
  • At requests that can be served and whose output tokens are the model's, for one commitment, up to 688,127 replies and 2^64 hash queries, against any verifier, the view is within statistical distance 2^-154 of the real one.
  • At a refused request the reply is the empty proof. With that, the same holds at every request, with one bit revealed for each: served or refused.

The theorem zeroKnowledgeOnCanServe is stated in terms of ZeroKnowledgeOn, for the requests that can be served and whose output tokens are the model's. The compiled system has no public parameters (PublicParameters := Unit, §4.3), so the simulator is initially given nothing about the weights. It may depend on the three public files, and a fitted model's scale file is derived from its weights; what these files reveal about the weights is not covered. Whether a request can be served depends on the weights, and this is not hidden: the chooser of requests may know the weights and is the same in both experiments.

In the theorem zeroKnowledgeOnCanServe, 2^64 bounds the verifier's hash queries and 688,127 bounds the replies under one commitment. Within these limits the error is at most 2^-154 (finalZeroKnowledgeError).

The simulator is given the bit of every request: up to 688,127 bits, at requests that the verifier picks. Over many requests the bits reveal what the model outputs, and the statement does not bound what they jointly reveal about the weights. In this theorem, 688,127 bounds the number of replies under one commitment; a reply to a refused request, which is the empty proof, also counts.

The theorem zeroKnowledgeAtEveryRequest, in full. For each public setup there is one simulator, fixed before the weights, such that for

  • all weights,
  • every chooser of requests, well-formed or not, whatever the model's result on them, and
  • every verifier with at most 2^64 hash queries and at most 688,127 replies under one commitment:

(1) the statistical distance between the verifier's view with the honest committer and prover and the simulator's output is at most finalZeroKnowledgeError, 2^-154;

(2) the simulator never answers one hash query in two ways.

Remark. The theorem is stated as ZeroKnowledgeBelowWhere (in the folded section below) for compile (flashProve setup) itself: at each request, the verifier is given the request and the compiled prover's reply (a proof or the empty proof), and nothing else.

What the simulator is told. The simulator is given the maximum number of replies, each request and, of the weights, only one bit for each request: served or refused (requestOutcome, §6.1). A reply is what the compiled prover returns: a proof or the empty proof (noProofForm). The strength of the statement depends only on this function (requestOutcome): its value is the only function of the weights that the simulator is handed with a request.

What the bit reveals. The bit depends on the weights, and it is not hidden (the statement gives it to the simulator):

  • For every well-formed request of its choice, a verifier learns whether the claimed output is the model's result. It infers the bit from the reply: a refused request gets an empty proof, and so, with small probability, does a served one (see §6.1 for the cases).
  • Hence, over many adaptively chosen requests, it learns the model's outputs on inputs of its choice: trying each candidate token for a prompt reveals the model's next token from this bit alone, unless all are refused.
  • An output that is the model's in the sense of §1 is refused if the model has no value at a later position in the window.
  • No statement bounds what many bits reveal together.

Public parameters. The type of public parameters of compile (flashProve setup) is Unit, so this system has none. Hence, in the experiment, the simulator of zeroKnowledgeAtEveryRequest is given the bits and nothing else about the weights (it may depend on the public files).

What a refusal does not reveal. For a well-formed request, a refusal does not reveal whether the model has no result or a result other than the claimed output. This is hidden only from a verifier that makes few requests:

  • A request's window of 1,024 tokens can itself be sent as a prompt, with one more token as the claimed output, which the run does not read.
  • A verifier that tries every candidate for that token and is refused each time learns that the model has no result on that window, and one that is served once learns that it has one (argued from the definitions; no theorem states it).
  • Each such search uses up to 202,048 (the vocabulary size) of the 688,127 replies.

Not covered by either theorem:

  • more than 688,127 replies or 2^64 hash queries;
  • what many bits reveal together;
  • what the public files themselves reveal about the weights, what is published alongside the commitment, and timing;
  • coins that are not fresh and uniform, several requests in one proof, a second commitment, and public files whose policy is not exact match (§4.4);
  • the simulator's running time;
  • a hash query before the commitment, and weights or public files chosen after the hash function is sampled;
  • whether the prover outputs any proof at all (that is the subject of completeOnCanServe; on its own, the property in each of these two theorems is satisfied by a prover that outputs nothing (§11)).

6.4 The honest committer and the honest prover of the compiled argument system

The theorem repliesFit, in full. For every public setup, three numerical conditions hold:

  • (1) finalReplyCount (688,127) is at most onlineRunsPerCopy setup, whose value is also the numeric literal 688,127; so (1) compares two literals, and (2) is what relates this number to a table;
  • (2) for each table, the number of columns counted for the proofs is at most the limit of 44,040,191 (TableBudgetFits: 62 + (furtherCopies + 1) · 62 on the first committed table, 62 + onlineRunsPerCopy setup · 64 on a copy);
  • (3) one run each of the honest sampler of commitment randomness, the honest committer and the honest prover together make at most 2^48 hash queries (WithinBudget, §6.1).

A copy. The committed table of weights is stored encoded, with random masks, and each proof opens some of its columns. Informally, one encoding supports only a limited number of openings before its masks are used up. A copy is a further encoding of the same table, with a link proof (compile, §4.3): a proof of the link IOP, which is meant to show that the copy decodes to the same index as the first encoding.

Condition (1) requires that the number of replies be at most the number of runs that the honest settings assign to one copy, because the prover samples its copy at random and keeps no count; condition (2) states that this many runs fit in one copy.

8. The model of hash functions

The model has one hash function, sampled uniformly at random among all functions from bit strings to 256 bits (the random oracle model). Every algorithm of the statements has query access to it; the statements bound the number of queries and, in zero knowledge, of replies, and nothing else. In the simulated experiment of zero knowledge the simulator answers the hash queries in the hash function's place.

Two types of algorithm, and where the hash function is sampled. RandomizedAlgorithm and DeterministicAlgorithm are both types of oracle algorithm: an algorithm of either type may query the hash function and continue with the answer, but neither fixes nor samples it. "Randomized" refers to the algorithm's own coins: a RandomizedAlgorithm may also sample random numbers of its own, whereas a DeterministicAlgorithm, the type of verify and of commit, may not. toRandomized views a deterministic algorithm as a step of an experiment and adds no randomness. In the statements on this page the hash function is sampled in Prob: the probability is taken over uniformHash, the uniform distribution on hash functions, and over the experiment's own random choices. evaluate instantiates the hash function with a concrete one, as in leanVerifier (§5).

The second hash function. FlashProve's second hash function is a different function: it is fixed, and it is part of the argument system. The model does not sample it. §5 states what the theorems assume about it (nothing) and what the Fiat–Shamir heuristic assumes about it.

Short names in the Lean code

The Lean code uses short names for some types, fields and variables, such as I, lam, enc and Pub. The folded section below lists some of them with their meanings.

The names, one by one
  • Ans: the out-of-domain answers.
  • aT: the offline IOP's round marking (which rounds a batch shares).
  • Bd: the type of a leaf's body (what the leaf contains in addition to its salt).
  • Digest: an output of the hash function (256 bits).
  • early: the early part early x of an instance x, which the first query of a Fiat–Shamir chain contains (HolographicProtocol, §3).
  • enc: several meanings, including the encoder in ConfigurationWithOutOfDomainSample (it maps a message and randomness to an encoding) and, as an argument of verifyDigestKey, Arg.digestKey and Rec.tokenArgumentSystem, the code of a key; the commitment is the hash function's answer at this code.
  • Further: the return type of the second public reading.
  • honestOfflineProver, honestLinkProver, honestOnlineBatchProver: §6.4.
  • I: the indices (for FlashProve, the committed data, derived from the weights).
  • Inst: either the namespace and folder of the integer model's definitions, or the instance (request file bytes, table key, reply file bytes).
  • Isk: the prover's key (the index and the tables of its stored copies); it does not contain the first table.
  • lam: the length in bits of a digest; 256 in the six theorems.
  • late: the number of the late round, if there is one; the query of that round contains the whole instance (HolographicProtocol, §3).
  • lowKey: the whole key's root and out-of-domain sample, for the compiled verifier.
  • lowPrf: the whole key and a proof, written as the compiled verifier's typed proof.
  • n: the encoding's length.
  • N: the batch size (the number of batch positions in one run of the online IOP).
  • ofUpload: a ZKCP oracle algorithm rewritten as a RandomizedAlgorithm.
  • Pub: either three public files as bytes (parameter, layout and scale files), or what the description takes from the three public files.
  • Rec: the out-of-domain sample (also a namespace: Rec.tokenArgumentSystem).
  • Seed: the out-of-domain seeds.
  • Wn: the witness type of the relations.
  • X: the instances (an instance is built from a request and further tokens).
  • ZKCP.Arg (ZKCP: zero-knowledge commit-and-prove): an argument consisting of three oracle algorithms: committer C, prover P, verifier V.

10. Sources

  • Third-party material in the Lean files that this page prints: lean/CREDITS.md. The HTML template, style sheet and script of this page: lean/scripts/statements-html/shell/ORIGIN.txt.

11. Limits

  • lean/LIMITS.md: all limits of the statements, numbered. A card gives only those most relevant to it.
  • lean/GAPS.md: the gaps between these statements and the programs.
  • lean/CHECK-RESULTS.md: the axioms that Lean lists for each theorem (at most the three standard axioms).
  • lean/CREDITS.md: whose work the Lean files follow.
  • docs/model.md: the symbols in the comments of the integer model (Appendix C).
  • Counts of declarations. The statement of the theorem sound depends on about 17,000 named declarations of this library. The general parts are small: Sound depends on 28, the model on about 160, blake2bHash on about 130, compile on about 720. Three declarations, whose dependencies overlap, account for nearly all the rest: FlashProve's description (flashProveDescription, about 12,000), the test on the public files (protocolDataWellFormed, about 9,100) and the honest provers and settings (honestProversAndSettings, about 16,000).
  • What is counted. Only names written in this library's source are counted: definitions, theorems and structures, with their fields and constructors, but not names that Lean generates or names from Mathlib. For a definition, the names used in its type and its value are counted; for a theorem, those used in its statement; and so on, transitively. The counts are computed by a program from the compiled library's record of the constants that each declaration uses, and are rounded to two digits. Of the about 17,000 names counted for the theorem sound, about 11,000 have their own declaration line, and about 9,100 of these are declared with def.
How to read the three kinds of statement together
  • Each statement on its own is satisfied by a useless argument system: soundness by a verifier that rejects everything (see the theorem card below), completeness by one that accepts everything, zero knowledge by a prover that outputs nothing.
  • The bounds are part of the statements. ε, α and ζ bound three different experiments and should not be compared with one another.
  • ε, α and ζ take values from 0 to ∞. A bound that is 1 or more makes its statement trivial.
  • A theorem about an argument system states each bound as an explicit function, except for zero knowledge: that theorem states that such a function exists and is at most 2^-154 for at most 2^64 hash queries and at most 688,127 replies. A single value of ε or ζ should be quoted together with the numbers of queries and of proofs at which it is evaluated.
